paraphrase: One should understand and break the bond. What did the hero (Mahāvīra) call the bond, and by knowing what does one break it? One who owns possessions, living or lifeless, or consents to others owning them, or who kills or has others kill, is not freed from suffering.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The opening verses of the Sūtrakṛtāṅga ('bujjhijja tiuṭṭijjā…').

paraphrase: Some say each self is complete (in its body), whether fool or wise; they exist, but after death they do not; there are no spontaneously born beings, no merit or demerit, no world beyond this; with the destruction of the body the embodied one is destroyed.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Śīlāṅka names this the tajjīva-taccharīra view.

paraphrase: Some boldly say that the self does not act or cause action: 'thus the self is a non-agent'; the Jain text says such teachers go from darkness to darkness.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify it with Sāṃkhya.

paraphrase: Some say there are five great elements and the self is a sixth, and that self and world are eternal: neither perishes, the non-existent does not arise, all things are of a fixed nature.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: Some fools speak of five aggregates lasting a moment, neither different nor the same (as the self), caused and uncaused; others say form is the four elements earth, water, fire and air.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. A Jain report of Buddhist views.

paraphrase: Each of these teachers claims that whoever adopts his view, at home, in the forest or as a renouncer, is freed from all suffering; the Jain text replies that they know neither the joint nor the dharma, do not cross the flood, saṃsāra, womb, birth, suffering or death, and wander again and again — so taught Nāyaputta Mahāvīra.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga. Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: Some say there are five great elements — earth, water, fire, air and space as fifth; from them arises a single (self), and with their destruction the embodied one is destroyed.

original.text: santi pañca mahabbhūyā, iham egesim āhiyā / puḍhavī āu teū vā, vāu āgāsapañcamā
original.edition: Suyagaḍa, GRETIL e-text (input Y. Ousaka & M. Yamazaki), checked locally
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted read-only for reference

notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Note: space (āgāsa) is the fifth element here, unlike the later Lokāyata's four.

paraphrase: As one earth-mound appears manifold, so, some say, the one knower (viṇṇu) appears manifold throughout the whole world; the Jain text calls these the words of dull men attached to violence.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify this as an Upaniṣadic one-self view.

paraphrase: It states and rejects rival views: that only the five elements exist and the self perishes with them; that there is one self appearing in many forms, as one earth appears as many things; that soul and body are one; that the self is inactive; that the self is a sixth, eternal element; and that there are only momentary aggregates (the Buddhist view). Those who hold them are not free from suffering.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The opponents' positions are reported by the Jain text (reported_by_opponent). Lesson-level ref; Śīlāṅka identifies the views (Cārvāka, Vedānta-like ekātmavāda, Sāṃkhya, Buddhism).

paraphrase: The fatalists say that pleasure and pain are neither caused by oneself nor by another but are determined by destiny (niyati); the text answers that such teachers, not understanding what is and is not caused by oneself, wander in saṃsāra.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Niyativāda (the Ājīvika position) as reported by the Jain text.

paraphrase: Some teach that beings, arising separately, experience pleasure and pain or lose their place, but that this suffering is neither self-made nor made by others: whether pleasure or pain, gained at the right time or not, it is determined by circumstance (saṅgaiya). The Jain text calls those who say this fools who think themselves wise, not knowing what is fixed and what is not fixed, and not freed from suffering.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify this as the Ājīvika niyativāda; the word saṅgaiya echoes DN 2's niyati-saṅgati-bhāva.

paraphrase: Some brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas each claim knowledge, yet know nothing of the beings in the world; like a barbarian repeating a non-barbarian's words without their meaning, the ignorant (annāṇiya) do not know the settled meaning; the inquiry of the ignorant cannot be settled in ignorance — unable to instruct themselves, how can they instruct others? Like a man lost in a forest following a guide equally lost, or the blind leading the blind, reasoners who follow their own speculation cannot escape suffering, like a bird from its cage.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: Another view, the kiriyāvāda of those 'who have left behind concern with karma': sin is incurred only by three means — acting oneself, commissioning another, and approving in mind; what is done unknowingly or without intent is not fully binding; purified by the intention within, one reaches nirvāṇa; even a father who, in need, kills and eats his son is not stained. The Jain text replies that those who sin in mind are not free of thought, and that such teachers are not restrained.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify it as a Buddhist doctrine of intention.

paraphrase: Some say the self is pure and sinless, yet through fondness for play (kiḍḍā-padosa) it falls again into fault; one who has become a restrained muni here later becomes sinless, 'as clear water becomes muddy and then clear again'.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators (Śīlāṅka, recalled with low confidence) ascribe this to the Trairāśikas, whom they identify with Gosāla's followers: the liberated soul returns to saṃsāra. The term khiḍḍāpadosika also names gods in DN 1.

paraphrase: Some say the world was made by the gods, others by Brahmā, by Īśvara, by the primal matter (pradhāna), by the self-born one (with the delusion spread by Māra, so that the world is impermanent), or that the world came from an egg; the Jain text says they do not know the truth — the world never perishes — and, not knowing the origin of suffering, cannot know how to stop it.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: This is the essence of wisdom: not to kill anything. Know that non-harm and equality (samaya) — just this much is the teaching.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The verse recurs at 1.11.10; verse-number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The 'Assembly' (Samavasaraṇa) lecture groups all other teachers under four doctrines — those who teach that action bears fruit (kriyāvāda), that it does not (akriyāvāda), that knowledge is useless (ajñānavāda), and that discipline or reverence alone saves (vinayavāda) — and says that the Jina, knowing the world and its beings, teaches beyond their partial views.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Later tradition (the niryukti) counts 363 views: 180 kriyāvāda, 84 akriyāvāda, 67 ajñānavāda, 32 vinayavāda.

paraphrase: There are four 'assemblies' (samosaraṇa) in which the disputants (pāvāduya) each speak: action (kiriya), non-action (akiriya), discipline (viṇaya) as third, and ignorance (annāṇa) as fourth.

original.text: cattāri samosaraṇāṇimāni, pāvāduyā jāiṃ puḍho vayanti / kiriyaṃ akiriyaṃ viṇayaṃ ti taiyaṃ, annāṇam āhaṃsu cautthameva
original.edition: Suyagaḍa, GRETIL e-text (input Y. Ousaka & M. Yamazaki), checked locally
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted read-only for reference

notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Suyagaḍa 1.12.1, checked.

paraphrase: The Jain teachers who know the world teach that suffering is self-made, not made by another, and that knowledge and conduct bring release; fools do not destroy karma by karma, the wise destroy karma by non-action; he who knows the self and the world, coming and not-coming, the eternal and the non-eternal, birth, death and rebirth, the influx (āsava) and its stopping (saṃvara), suffering and its wearing away (nijjarā) — he is fit to teach the doctrine of action (kiriyavāda).
notes: Suyagaḍa 1.12.11–22, checked.

paraphrase: The ignorant (annāṇiya), though they think themselves skilled, are not beyond doubt; unskilled, they speak to the unskilled and, without reflection, speak falsely.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Suyagaḍa 1.12.2, checked.

paraphrase: The many 'disciplinarians' (veṇaiya), thinking the true untrue and calling the bad good, when asked, name their doctrine 'discipline' (viṇaya).
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Suyagaḍa 1.12.3, checked.

paraphrase: The deniers of action (akiriyavāī), fearing to admit consequences, say nothing is established and deny action; mixing their words they fall into confusion; 'the sun does not rise or set, the moon does not wax or wane, the waters do not flow, the winds do not blow: the whole world is barren and fixed'. Like a blind man with a lamp who cannot see forms, they do not see action though it exists.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Suyagaḍa 1.12.4–8, checked. The 'barren (vañjha) and fixed' world echoes the vañjhā kūṭaṭṭhā of Pakudha in DN 2.

paraphrase: Many study the eightfold science — year-lore, dreams, marks, portents, bodily signs and omens — and claim to know the future; some omens come true, for others the knowledge fails; not studying true knowledge, they speak of release through lore alone.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Suyagaḍa 1.12.9–10, checked.

paraphrase: Wake up! Why do you not wake up? Enlightenment is hard to gain in the next world; the nights that pass do not return, and human life is not easily obtained again.
speaker: Ṛṣabha to his sons (per the commentary)
notes: The commentators set this 'Vaitālīya' lecture in Ṛṣabha's mouth addressing his sons; moderate confidence on that framing.

paraphrase: The lecture on women (Strīparijñā) warns the monk of the ways in which women tempt and bind a renouncer and describes the servitude of the monk who falls; it counsels avoiding intimacy and solitude with them.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Recorded as the text states it (addressed to male monks); lecture-level ref.

paraphrase: The praise of Mahāvīra (Vīrastuti): asked by monks, brāhmaṇas and householders, Sudharman describes the Jñātṛ son as the all-knowing, the best of those who have conquered, like Mount Meru among mountains, the ocean among waters, and the one who taught the dharma after knowing it himself.
speaker: Sudharman
notes: Lecture-level ref ('pucchissu ṇaṃ samaṇā māhaṇā ya…').

paraphrase: In the parable of the lotus, the first man who fails to pluck the lotus holds that the soul is the body (tajjīva-taccharīra): 'upward from the soles of the feet, downward from the tips of the hair, bounded by the skin — this is the soul; when the body dies it does not live'; no one can draw the soul out of the body and show it, like a sword from its sheath or a fibre from a reed; there is no other world, no good or bad deed; the second man holds the five-element view, the third that Īśvara or the self is the cause of all, the fourth that all is fixed by destiny.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Book 2 is not available locally; from memory, chapter-level ref. The skin-bounded formula is verified in the parallel Isibhāsiyāiṃ 20.

paraphrase: The parable of the lotus (Puṇḍarīka): a great white lotus stands in the middle of a pond; four men from the four directions wade in to pluck it and sink in the mud; a monk standing on the bank calls, 'Rise, O lotus!' and it comes. The pond is the world, the mud desires, the four men the teachers of the soul-is-body view, of the five elements, of a creator-self and of fate; the monk is the one who teaches the true dharma; the lotus is the king (the person to be freed).
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Chapter-level ref.

paraphrase: Gosāla accuses Mahāvīra of having changed: once he wandered alone, now he preaches to crowds for gain; and he states the Ājīvika rule that an ascetic living alone may use cold water, seeds, food prepared for him and women without sin. Ārdraka answers that Mahāvīra is the same alone or amid crowds, and that those who use these things are householders, not ascetics.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Ārdrakīya chapter; not available locally; from memory.

paraphrase: Buddhist monks tell Ārdraka that one who roasts a cake of oil-seed thinking it is a man incurs the sin of killing, while one who roasts a child thinking it a gourd does not; Ārdraka rejects this doctrine of intention as unfit for the restrained.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). From memory; chapter-level ref.

paraphrase: Elephant-ascetics (hatthitāvasa) say that by killing one elephant a year for food they harm fewer lives than those who gather grain; Ārdraka answers that they still kill a five-sensed being and are no better than householders.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). From memory; chapter-level ref.

paraphrase: Ārdraka, on his way to Mahāvīra, answers in turn Gośāla (who charges Mahāvīra with inconsistency for once living alone and now teaching crowds), Buddhist monks (who say intention alone matters, so that roasting a child mistaken for a gourd would bring no sin), brāhmaṇas (who praise feeding two thousand snātakas), Vedāntin ascetics, and hermits who kill one elephant a year to live without harming many small beings; he refutes each by the standard of non-harm and right knowledge.
speaker: Ārdraka
notes: The opponents' positions are reported by the Jain text.

paraphrase: At Nālandā, Udaka Peḍhālaputta, a monk of Pārśva's line, questions Gautama on whether the layman's limited vow of non-harm is sound when beings change their state; Gautama answers, and Udaka accepts Mahāvīra's fivefold discipline.
speaker: Gautama and Udaka
